Markup in text: **bold**, *italic*, and [[words|colour]] to tie words to a figure colour (parcel = orange rising air, env = violet surrounding air, dew = teal dew point). The lessons tell no story: the radio talks and the locals asking forecast questions (by forecast "id") are in data/radio.
title: Rising air and heaps
teaches: Why rising air cools, where the cloud base sits, and why unstable air builds heaps of cumulus while stable air lies flat

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Air cools when it rises: there is less air above pressing down, so it expands, and expanding air cools, by about 10 °C per kilometre.
Its dew point falls only about 2 °C per kilometre, so the gap closes as it climbs. Where they meet is the **cloud base**.
So most clouds mark places where air is rising.
Air warmer than its surroundings is lighter, so it rises; cooler air sinks.

In **unstable** air a rising bubble stays warmer than the air around it and keeps going, building heaps: **cumulus**. In **stable** air it is pushed back, so cloud forms only when a whole layer is lifted or chilled: flat **stratus**.

blocks.text: Fog forms where air touches the cold ground. Most clouds, though, float a kilometre or more overhead, in air that never touches anything cold. The sky’s other way of cooling air, and by far the more common one, is lifting it.
To see why lifting cools air down, follow a single blob of air on its way up. In meteorology, a blob like this is called a **parcel**.

Of course, a parcel has no skin around it, and at its edges it is always mixing with the surrounding air. Even so, air genuinely moves in distinct blobs. A bubble of warm air rising off a sunny field can be a few hundred metres across and hold together for many minutes; hawks and glider pilots find these bubbles and circle inside them to climb. Because a blob that size mixes only around its outer edges, its core carries its own temperature and moisture upward. Treating a rising bubble as a self-contained parcel is a simplification, like a physicist’s frictionless ball, but it captures the essential physics.

Air near the ground is compressed by the weight of all the air piled above it, which comes to about ten tonnes on every square metre. We don’t feel crushed because the air and fluids inside our bodies push outward just as hard as the atmosphere pushes in. If you climb one kilometre, you leave about a tenth of the atmosphere below you, so there is a tenth less weight on top and the surrounding pressure is a tenth weaker.

When a parcel of air rises into that lower pressure, the air inside it is still at the higher pressure it had lower down, pushing outward harder than the air around it pushes in, so the parcel expands until its internal pressure drops to match the air outside.

When air expands, it cools. You have probably felt the opposite effect when pumping up a bicycle tyre, where compressing the air makes the pump warm. You can see expansion cooling directly if you pop open a bottle of fizzy drink: as the pressure drops, the gas in the neck expands, cools past its dew point, and forms a brief wisp of fog.

Temperature is simply a measure of how fast molecules are jostling around. As a rising parcel expands, its molecules spend energy pushing the surrounding air out of the way, so they come away moving a little more slowly. Nothing cold has touched the parcel; it cools because its own molecules did the work of expanding.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air rising from the ground. Nothing is added or taken away: the same molecules just spread out.

blocks.text: As long as no cloud has formed yet, a rising parcel cools at a steady rate of about 10 °C for every kilometre it climbs (9.8 °C, to be exact). This rate isn’t a rough average across different days. It follows directly from how hard gravity pulls on the atmosphere and how much heat energy air stores, so it is the same every day.

The parcel’s dew point also drops as it climbs, but much more slowly, at about 2 °C per kilometre. The parcel hasn’t lost any water, yet as it expands, the same water vapour is spread across a larger volume, leaving fewer grams of vapour in each cubic metre. Less crowded vapour has a lower dew point, just like sliding the water control down a little in the jar figure.

In a [[rising parcel|parcel]], two temperatures are converging: its actual temperature falls by about 10 °C per kilometre, while its [[dew point|dew]] falls by about 2 °C per kilometre. The gap between them closes by about 8 °C for every kilometre the parcel climbs.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air at ground level, 24 °C with a dew point of 12 °C.
blocks.task: Lift the air until it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Where the two lines meet, the parcel has cooled to its dew point. Its vapour condenses into droplets, and the parcel becomes cloud. That height is the **cloud base**, and you can work it out directly from the ground readings. Because the gap closes by 8 °C every kilometre, each degree of gap at the ground takes about 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 metres of lift to close. At the ground this morning, the gap is 24 − 12 = 12 °C, which puts the cloud base at about 12 × 125 = 1,500 metres above the ground.

You can see this relationship all summer. On a muggy day, the dew point starts out close to the air temperature, so rising air reaches condensation quickly and clouds form low. On a dry day, the gap is wide and cloud bases sit high. Try moving the dew point slider to see how the cloud base shifts.

Most clouds mark places where air has risen and cooled below its dew point. (Fog, from the last lesson, is the exception: air cooled right where it sits.) What makes one cloud look so different from another is mostly *how* the air rose: in separate rising bubbles, or all together as a wide layer.

Why does air sometimes rise in isolated bubbles and other times stay in a flat layer? Suppose you give a parcel of air a small push upward. On some days, that parcel will keep rising on its own. On other days, it will sink right back down to where it started. Which way the atmosphere behaves on a given day determines almost everything about the clouds that form.

Recall from the last lesson why air rises on its own at all: a warm parcel is less dense than the cooler air around it, so the heavier air slides underneath and buoys it upward, like a hot-air balloon. A cold parcel is denser, and sinks.

While a rising dry parcel always cools at about 10 °C per kilometre, the [[air around it|env]] also changes temperature with height, and that surrounding profile varies from day to day. Averaged over the whole earth and year, the atmosphere gets colder by about 6.5 °C per kilometre of altitude. On a hot afternoon when strong sunshine bakes the ground, the lowest kilometre or two can get colder with height by more than 10 °C per kilometre. On a clear morning after the ground has cooled all night, the temperature may drop much more slowly with height, or even get warmer as you go up: the **inversion** from the last lesson.

To see what happens to a nudged parcel, compare the two cooling rates. Push a parcel up a kilometre, and it cools at 10 °C per kilometre on the way. If the surrounding air gets colder with height *faster* than that, say at 12 °C per kilometre, the parcel arrives at its new altitude warmer and less dense than its new neighbours. Because it is warmer and lighter, it keeps rising on its own, and the higher it climbs, the greater its temperature lead becomes. Meteorologists call this **unstable** air.

If instead the surrounding air gets colder with height *more slowly* than 10 °C per kilometre, say at 5 °C per kilometre, the nudged parcel arrives colder and denser than its new neighbours. Being heavier than the air around it, it sinks back down to where it started. That air is **stable**. Notice that stable and unstable describe the temperature profile of the surrounding sky on that day, which governs what happens to any parcel that gets nudged.

blocks.caption: Two days, two skies. Each bubble is nudged up one kilometre and cools 10 °C; what decides its fate is the air around it.

blocks.text: Here is a picture to hold on to: a ball on uneven ground. Nudge a ball sitting at the bottom of a bowl, and it rolls back to where it started. That is **stable** air: the nudged bubble ends up colder than its neighbours and sinks back.

Now balance the ball on top of a hill. The slightest nudge, and it rolls away, faster and faster the farther it goes. That is **unstable** air: the nudged bubble ends up warmer than its neighbours, and the higher it climbs, the bigger its lead.

In the figure, the ball rolling to the right stands for the bubble rising. The shape of the ground is set by the air around the bubble: the Air slider turns the bowl into a hilltop, and the two temperatures beside the bubble tell you which way the ball will roll.

blocks.caption: A bubble of air nudged upward. Its own temperature is orange; the air around it is violet.
blocks.task: Nudge the bubble once in stable air and once in unstable air.

blocks.text: Those two behaviours give the sky its two basic textures. In unstable air, warm bubbles shoot up on their own wherever heated ground gives them a start, and each bubble builds its own cloud, forming **heaps**. In stable air, nothing climbs by itself. Air turns to cloud only if something does the cooling for it, to a whole layer at once: wind pushing the layer steadily up a mountain slope, or cold ground chilling the air resting on it. When a wide layer is cooled gently all together, it forms a flat **sheet**.

Nearly every cloud in the low sky is a heap, a sheet, or a combination of the two, such as heaps that flatten out against a stable layer into a lumpy sheet. Later lessons cover those combinations, along with the high, icy wisps that form near the top of the weather, ten kilometres up. You have already met the pure sheet, stratus. Now for the pure heap.

Sunlight passes through clear air almost without warming it. The ground absorbs the sunlight instead, and the warm ground heats the air touching it. Different surfaces warm up at different rates: dark rock, bare fields, and roofs get hot quickly, while a lake or a damp forest spends much of the sun’s energy evaporating water and stays cooler.

Over a hot patch of ground, the air warms, becomes less dense than the cooler air around it, and eventually breaks free to rise as a bubble called a **thermal**. A thermal behaves just like the parcel we followed earlier, cooling at 10 °C per kilometre as it expands and closing the gap to its dew point. Where temperature and dew point meet, water vapour condenses into droplets and from there up the thermal becomes visible as a heap of cloud: a **cumulus**.

blocks.caption: A sunny morning over farm country. Thermals rise from the warmest ground.
blocks.task: Bring the sun up until two clouds have formed.

blocks.text: In the figure, notice that every heap starts at the same height, giving cumulus clouds **flat bases** all at one level. You might expect a bubble rising off the hottest rock to start out much warmer and reach its dew point much higher up. In practice, by mid-morning the rising thermals have stirred the lowest kilometre of the sky so thoroughly that the air across the valley has nearly uniform temperature and moisture. A bubble breaks away as soon as it is a degree or so warmer than its surroundings, which changes its condensation height by only a hundred metres or so. Seen from across the valley, the cloud bases line up along a flat level.

Moving the **moisture** slider shifts that level up or down. Humid air starts with a small gap between temperature and dew point, so its cloud bases are low; dry air starts with a wide gap, so its bases are high. Because a thermal only keeps rising while it remains warmer than the air around it, on very dry days the rising bubbles lose their temperature lead and stop climbing before they ever reach their dew point. The thermals then stay completely invisible, leaving a blue, cloudless sky that is still bumpy for gliders.

Why doesn’t a rising bubble stop once it reaches the cloud base? When water evaporates, it absorbs heat energy, which is why sweat cools your skin as it dries. When water vapour condenses back into liquid droplets inside a cloud, it releases that stored heat back into the surrounding air. Meteorologists call it **latent heat**, from the Latin for hidden. That heat warms the cloudy parcel from within, so above the cloud base the rising air cools by only about 5 °C per kilometre instead of 10 °C.

Whether the parcel keeps rising still depends on comparing its cooling rate with the air around it. Often the surrounding air a kilometre or two up gets colder by 6 or 7 °C per kilometre. A dry thermal cooling at 10 °C per kilometre would quickly become colder than that surrounding air and stop rising. A cloudy thermal cooling at 5 °C per kilometre stays warmer than its surroundings, so its buoyancy increases and it keeps billowing upward in bright, cauliflower-like towers.

So the same sky can be stable for a clear bubble and unstable for a cloudy one. Air that cools 6 or 7 °C per kilometre would stop a dry thermal, but not a cloudy one. And below the cloud base, a thermal is not fighting that air at all: on a sunny afternoon the thermals themselves have stirred the lowest kilometre until it cools at about 10 °C per kilometre, just like the bubbles, so a bubble only a degree warmer than the rest keeps that lead all the way up to its dew point. Below the base the sun does the work; above it, the heat from condensing water does.

blocks.title: The stability test, in full
points: Compare two rates: how fast the **air around** gets colder as you go up, and how fast a **rising bubble** cools.
A clear bubble cools about 10 °C per kilometre. A cloudy one cools only about 5, because condensing water warms it.
If the air around cools faster than the bubble, the bubble stays warmer and keeps rising: **unstable**. If slower, the bubble ends up colder and sinks back: **stable**.
So air that cools 6 or 7 °C per kilometre is stable for a clear bubble but unstable for a cloudy one. That is why a cumulus, once it forms, can keep on growing.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height: the air around, and a bubble before and after it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Between the cumulus clouds, the sky stays clear. Every bit of air that rises in a thermal must be replaced by air sinking somewhere else. As the air between the thermals sinks into higher pressure, it is compressed and warms by 10 °C per kilometre, moving its temperature further above its dew point so no cloud can form.

blocks.caption: A fair-weather cumulus, and the air moving around it.

blocks.text: Small cumulus scattered across a blue sky are the best weather there is, and they are called fair-weather cumulus. They appear with the morning sun and fade around sunset, when the ground stops heating the air and the thermals shut down.

Put the two lessons side by side and you have the sky’s two basic textures. Stratus is air chilled in a still, stable layer; cumulus is air that bubbles up on its own because the sky around it is unstable. Every other cloud in this workbook is one of those two ideas, or a mix of them, at one of three heights, which the next lesson sorts out.
The photos below are real skies. Name each one: cumulus heaps or a stratus blanket.
**Cumulus**: separate heaps with flat bases, bright tops, and blue sky between them. **Stratus**: a flat, uniform grey layer with no gaps, often hiding the hills.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: On a muggy morning the temperature is 24 °C and the dew point 20 °C. Will the cumulus bases be low or high today?
options: There will be no cloud: the air is too warm
items.why: A gap of 4 °C between temperature and dew point closes after about 4 × 125 = 500 metres of lift, so humid air makes low bases.

items.question: Small, flat-bottomed heaps popped up mid-morning and have stayed small all day, drifting across a blue sky. Is it safe to leave cut hay out to dry?
options: Yes: fair-weather cumulus, and they will fade by evening
No: heaps like these mean rain by evening
items.why: Small cumulus that stay small are thermals that run into stable air a little above their bases, so they cannot grow tall. They come with the morning sun and fade when the ground stops heating the air: fair weather.

learned: Rising air expands and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre, while its dew point falls by about 2 °C per kilometre, closing the gap between them by 8 °C per kilometre.
The cloud base sits about 125 m above the ground for each degree Celsius between the surface temperature and the dew point, forming low on humid days and high on dry ones.

Air is unstable when the surrounding atmosphere gets colder with height faster than a rising bubble cools (10 °C per kilometre in clear air, or about 5 °C per kilometre inside a cloud). A nudged bubble keeps rising on its own, building cumulus heaps with flat bases and bright tops.
In stable air, a nudged bubble becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back down. It forms cloud only when a whole layer is lifted or chilled together, making flat sheets like stratus.
next: Next lesson covers the rest of the low sky, from lumpy sheets that bring dry weather to thick grey layers that bring steady rain.

rising-air.title: Rising air
rising-air.text: Rising air expands into the lower pressure aloft and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre while its dew point falls by about 2 °C per kilometre, so the gap between them closes by 8 °C per kilometre. The cloud base forms about 125 m up for each degree Celsius between the temperature and dew point at the ground: low on humid days, high on dry ones.

stability.title: Stable and unstable air
stability.text: A rising dry parcel cools at 10 °C per kilometre. If the surrounding air gets colder with height faster than that, a lifted parcel ends up warmer than its neighbours and keeps rising on its own; this is unstable air, which builds heaps. If the surrounding air cools more slowly with height, or warms with height in an inversion, a lifted parcel ends up colder than its neighbours and sinks back down; this is stable air, which turns to cloud only when a whole layer is cooled together into flat sheets.

cumulus.title: Cumulus
cumulus.text: Separate heaps of cloud with flat bases and bright, rounded tops, built by rising thermals on sunny days. Small ones indicate fair weather, while towers still growing tall at midday can bring afternoon showers.
